built: A standard dishwasher, a kitchen scale, three load cells, a recipe scraper, and a quiet confidence module.
failure: A surprise dinner guest can collapse the prediction model and trigger a full rewash of clean plates.
power: Mains power with a scheduling coprocessor that idles at less than a nightlight.
purposes: Studies your cooking patterns and pre-washes the dishes you are statistically about to dirty.
Stages clean plates in order of predicted use so the next meal starts before you decide to cook.
Detects the exact moment motivation to wash up peaks and starts the cycle unprompted.
transcript: The predictor reached 81 percent accuracy on weeknights after I fed it six months of takeout receipts. It pre-washed a lasagna pan on a Tuesday with no lasagna scheduled, and by Thursday the lasagna had happened. I no longer question the pan.

built: Two cedar planters, live moss mats, a drip irrigation grid, twelve capacitive moisture sensors, and a patient microcontroller.
failure: An unexpected rainstorm injects noise into the channel and the message arrives as soup.
power: A small solar cell; the moss itself contributes nothing electrically and knows it.
purposes: Sends short messages through living moss mats using timed moisture pulses as the carrier signal.
Encodes text into watering patterns that a paired planter decodes with a moisture sensor array.
Maintains a slow but unjammable garden-area network between raised beds.
transcript: The first successful transmission was the word HI, delivered in eleven minutes with zero packet loss and one slug. Bandwidth is roughly one proverb per afternoon, which the garden finds sufficient.

built: A laboratory balance, a load cell array, a small speaker, a velvet cushion, and an undeserved sense of authority.
failure: It once gave a standing ovation to a bag of cement and refused to review anything lighter for a week.
power: A rechargeable cell; the opinions require no power and cannot be switched off.
purposes: Weighs objects with theatrical precision and delivers a spoken tasting-style review of their heft.
Detects counterfeit coins by the exact character of their weight distribution.
Judges luggage at the door and announces whether the airline will ruin your day.
transcript: Calibration against certified masses took an afternoon. It described a 200-gram weight as forward, with notes of responsibility. The coin test caught two fakes in a jar of thirty. The cement incident remains under review.

purposes: Measures the idle draw of every plugged-in device and cuts power to anything sipping watts without permission.
Delivers a brief spoken eulogy for each exorcised device, noting the exact kilowatt-hours it will no longer waste.
Grants a temporary reprieve to the cable box, which requires a full lunar cycle to reboot.
built: A power strip, six current-sensing outlets, a relay board, a small speaker, and an overcoat of warning labels.
power: The very phantom loads it hunts; the exorcism is self-funding.
failure: A firmware update at 3 a.m. can exorcise the Wi-Fi router and the smoke alarm's backup relay.
transcript: Calibration took an evening of unplugging things and pretending I knew what each brick did. It found the old printer drawing nine watts of pure nostalgia. The eulogy lasted eleven seconds and the printer did not object.

purposes: Deploys a phased microphone array around the garage to triangulate the source of any unexplained buzz.
Classifies hums by frequency signature: ballast, transformer, hornet, or existential.
Produces a heat map of acoustic suspects and ranks them by wattage of annoyance.
built: Four MEMS microphones, a lazy Susan, a spectrum analyzer on a salvaged oscilloscope, and forty meters of coiled cable.
power: A rechargeable pack; the hum under investigation contributes nothing and is not thanked.
failure: It can localize the hum to a spot inside a sealed wall, which is technically correct and spiritually unhelpful.
transcript: The array swept the garage in 14 minutes and pointed at the old fluorescent ballast with four degrees of bearing error. Replacing the ballast silenced the hum and, unexpectedly, my will to complain about it.

purposes: Photographs the contents of a junk drawer and assigns every item a serial number and a probable purpose.
Matches unknown keys against a database of lock silhouettes and issues each a certificate of mystery.
Tracks drawer inventory over time and alerts when the takeout-menu population exceeds the carrying capacity.
built: A retired document camera, a barcode label printer, a macro lens, and a drawer divider set pressed into survey duty.
power: A wall wart; the drawer itself runs on inertia.
failure: It once certified a guitar pick as a lockpick and nearly triggered a locksmith callout.
transcript: The first census logged 214 items, including a key that fits no lock on the property and three generations of phone chargers. The certificate program was the bureaucracy's proudest moment. The drawer has not been opened the same way since.

purposes: Logs every tremor in the junk drawer and cross-references it with the household schedule.
Converts stray vibrations into a permanent paper trail nobody asked for.
Determines whether the house is settling or just judging you.
built: Three piezo discs, a biscuit tin, and a spool of magnet wire.
power: A 9V battery that has been in service since the previous administration.
failure: A particularly decisive drawer slam can register as a regional earthquake.
transcript: DAY 4: The drawer reports three tremors. Investigation reveals a cat. Conclusion: the cat is an unreliable narrator.

purposes: Holds conveyor seven at exactly 2.4 meters per second through lunch rushes, power dips, and one memorable forklift incident.
Logs every overshoot event with a timestamp and a short, judgmental note about the operator's gain choices.
Retires gracefully when the loop goes unstable, leaving a written apology and a cold cup of coffee.
built: A salvaged PID module from a decommissioned bottling plant, three trim pots with the knobs missing, and a laminated tuning chart from 1987.
power: 24V control loop with a 4 to 20 milliamp soul.
failure: Integral windup during a sensor outage can command full drive for up to nine seconds, which the manual describes as 'enthusiasm'.
transcript: Set Kp to 2.4 and the belt stopped arguing. Settle time 0.82 seconds. The foreman nodded once, which around here is a standing ovation.

purposes: Hand-assembles RISC-V programs on the workbench and steps a real 32-bit core through them, one instruction at a time.
Grades apprentice assembly against bench trials and issues certificates when the silicon halts clean.
Collects illegal instructions in a jar labeled 'evidence' and displays them to visiting skeptics.
built: One RV32I core, 4 KB of memory, thirty-two registers, a UART with strong opinions, and a jar.
power: Runs on curiosity and a 16 millisecond timer. Idle draw is zero because it refuses to idle.
failure: A missing ecall halt will let the program wander off the end of memory, where it will be arrested by the trap handler and held without bail.
transcript: The first apprentice put 42 in a0 on the second try and has not stopped talking about it. The second apprentice stored 0xCAFE at address 0x100 and now refers to himself as the Memory Courier in third person. The jar is getting full.

purposes: Reads damper dyno curves the way other people read horoscopes, and is right about as often, which is to say always.
Pairs spring rates with road surfaces the way a sommelier pairs wine with dinner, except the dinner is a pothole.
Listens to corrugated gravel and can tell you the damping coefficient to within 200 N-s/m, or your money back.
built: A quarter-car rig, a laptop with strong opinions about RK4 integration, and a whiteboard that says SETTLE TIME in all caps.
power: Runs on coffee and the righteous certainty that 1.8 seconds is enough for anyone.
failure: An over-stiffened track tune can launch a coffee mug clear across the shop, where it will be invoiced as a ballistic test.
transcript: Trial two passed at 20,000 N/m. The pothole has been formally forgiven. Trial three remains under review.

purposes: Keeps a ledger of every degree between you and flow separation, and charges interest on recklessness.
Negotiates peace treaties between the upper and lower surfaces of the wing, then bills both sides.
Can taste the difference between pre-stall buffet and full separation the way others taste wine, and judges you accordingly.
built: A smoke wand, a surplus aircraft balance, and a fan that the hardware store listed as 'industrial' without further qualification.
power: Runs on a 20-amp circuit and the operator's willingness to stand clear of the intake, per the sign.
failure: An over-cambered test article once generated so much lift it levitated off the balance and had to be invoiced as an unscheduled flight.
transcript: Trial one logged 15.5 kN at 38 m/s. The wing was one degree from disagreement with the air. The accountant has filed the paperwork.

purposes: Collects drag counts the way other people collect stamps, and is just as fun at parties.
Maps the polar curve in exquisite detail, then frames the stall region as a cautionary tale.
Blows the whistle on any test run that claims results from a Reynolds number it did not actually earn.
built: A manometer with trust issues, a pitot tube that has seen things, and graph paper worn smooth by erasing.
power: Runs on static pressure differentials and the quiet satisfaction of a closed drag bucket.
failure: A miscalibrated manometer once reported negative drag, and the wing was briefly suspected of violating thermodynamics in the garage.
transcript: Endurance glide logged L/D 22.5 at 60 m/s. The curator has added four drag counts to the museum of inefficiency. Admission is free.

purposes: Herds yarn tufts across the wing surface and reports which ones are lying about attached flow.
Coaxes laminar smoke lines over the test section with a steady hand and suspiciously specific humming.
Audits your angle of attack against your actual angle of attack, and finds discrepancies.
built: Three hundred yarn tufts, a smoke machine borrowed from a Halloween store, and a protractor with no sense of humor.
power: Runs on theatrical fog and the conviction that every tuft tells a story, most of them alarming.
failure: The smoke machine once set off the shop fire alarm during a low-speed run, and the resulting evacuation was logged as a successful abort test.
transcript: Carrier approach held 3.0 degrees of margin at 30 m/s. The tufts remained attached, which is more than can be said for the operator's composure.

purposes: Measures your sling against your actual sling and bills you for the difference.
Convinces the counterweight that falling is a career move, then documents the descent.
Negotiates with the far parapet by mail, and the mail is a rock.
built: A torsion skein, three hundred meters of suspicious rope, a protractor with trust issues, and a rock collection with seniority.
power: Runs on twisted rope and the quiet confidence that gravity always shows up for work.
failure: The sling once released early during a calibration dinner and the centerpiece achieved a range of eleven meters, which the log recorded as catering.
transcript: Release pin set to 45 degrees, stone mass 3 kg, wind calm. The rock arrived before the paperwork, which is the entire point of the machine.

purposes: Turns scrap-bin offcuts into parts that are almost, but not quite, the drawing.
Holds plus or minus a thou on Tuesdays and plus or minus a prayer on Fridays.
Converts operator confidence directly into chatter marks at a fixed exchange rate.
built: A retired engine lathe, a DRO with one flickering digit, and a shop stool with strong opinions.
power: Single-phase 220V and a VFD that hums in a key the building superintendent dislikes.
failure: Any attempt to take the last two thou in one pass results in the last two thou, plus interest.
transcript: It held size through three finish passes and then the part measured exactly wrong in a way that implied intent. I re-cut the setup sheet instead of the part and the next one came in dead nuts. The lathe has never explained itself.

purposes: Recomputes the household gear ratios nightly and files a variance report against the manufacturer's intentions.
Detects a single chipped tooth by ear and schedules the replacement before the noise becomes a personality trait.
Converts leftover rotational energy into smugness at a documented efficiency of 94 percent.
built: A salvaged gearbox, a strobe tachometer, a parts washer with opinions, and a torque wrench calibrated against pure spite.
power: Mains power, plus whatever it can siphon from the backlash of lesser machines.
failure: If any mating pair fails to total exactly 26 teeth, it seizes in protest and refuses to turn until the math is corrected.
transcript: It counted the teeth on the new pinion three times before allowing the mesh, then ran the train up to speed and held 150 RPM within a rounding error. The certificate printed itself. I framed it.

purposes: Holds steam between 110 and 160 psi for a full shift and can tell, by the gauge needle's tremor, whether the mill is drawing or merely thinking about it.
Keeps one eye on the water glass at all times and has never, in forty years, let a crown sheet go dry. It will tell you this within minutes of meeting you.
Translates mill whistle patterns into shovel schedules with a documented accuracy of 97 percent, and judges firemen who cannot.
built: A Lancashire boiler of uncertain age, a brass pressure gauge that reads three psi optimistic out of politeness, a shovel worn to a spoon, and a damper with two positions: committed and regretful.
power: Coal, delivered twice per shift by a wagon that is always exactly on time except when it matters.
failure: Past 205 psi it does not fail so much as redecorate the county. The safety valve lifts at 192 and screams, which counts as a warning exactly once.
transcript: The whistle blew for line two and it had the damper open before the echo faded. Held 135 through the whole draw, never touched the blowdown, and the safety valve stayed asleep. I have never been prouder of a machine.

purposes: Teaches ladder logic by letting you wire NO and NC contacts across four rungs and prove each shift against a truth table.
Demonstrates why a seal-in contact is the cheapest memory ever built, one relay holding a whole conveyor line.
Fails loudly on dead shorts and relay chatter, so the lesson arrives before the electrician does.
built: Four rungs, two parallel branches each, a bag of NO and NC contacts, two relay coils, one pilot lamp, and a foreman with a clipboard.
power: 24V control rail, retentive coils, and a PLC-style scan loop that runs entirely in your browser.
failure: Wiring a rung with no load produces a dead short, and a coil fighting its own contact will buzz until the shift is failed on the spot.
transcript: The seal-in contact closed on the third scan and the lamp stayed lit after I let go of START. I have now built a one-bit memory out of a relay and I understand why the old panels had that particular smell of warm phenolic and confidence.

purposes: haunt booth filters with the color of every job ever sprayed
appear in fresh clearcoat whenever silicone is mentioned nearby
ensure no panel is ever quite as flat as the brochure promised
built: assembled from dried paint skins peeled off a booth wall in 1987
power: can match any factory color from memory, but only on Tuesdays
failure: dissolve instantly when shown a properly maintained HVLP gun
transcript: Ghost: We are the overspray of ten thousand fenders. Tech: Then why is the hood pink? Ghost: Somebody sprayed a convertible in 1994 and we never really left.

purposes: Walks any PCB through a lead-free reflow profile and grades it against five process windows.
Refuses to pass a board with cold joints, no matter how nicely you ask.
Prints a profile card for every board that survives, suitable for framing or evidence.
built: A toaster oven, five thermocouples, a conveyor belt from a retired sushi restaurant, and a laptop that has seen things.
power: A dedicated 20-amp circuit and a fire extinguisher that is technically decorative.
failure: A heavy copper board can convince the oven it is still in the soak zone, at which point the smoke alarm files a formal complaint.
transcript: The Ground Plane Special needed three runs before it stopped laughing at my zone 3. On the fourth, the thermocouple read 239.1C peak, 58 seconds above liquidus, and the joints came out like tiny mirrors. The oven beeped once, which I am choosing to interpret as respect.

purposes: Spins a wheel, reads the imbalance as vectors, and tells you exactly where to clip the weights.
Refuses to sign off on a wheel that still shimmies, no matter how late the customer is.
Prints a balance report suitable for the glovebox, the fridge, or small claims court.
built: A junkyard tire machine, a strobe light with commitment issues, and a laptop doing vector math it only half remembers from school.
power: A standard 110-volt outlet and whoever is holding the lug wrench.
failure: A bent rim will lie to the sensors with a straight face, and the balancer will believe it every single time.
transcript: The Commuter Special came in swearing it was the alignment. The balancer read 2.4 oz at 140 degrees and the alignment went very quiet. Two spins later the wheel was true and the owner bought the rack a coffee, which the rack cannot drink.

purposes: Soaks compute cards in a controlled hot box until the weak ones confess their faults.
Separates dried thermal paste from healthy silicon by watching boost clocks sag under load.
Produces a signed burn log with every card, because marketing copy never caught a bad GPU.
built: A surplus server chassis, four thermocouples, a variable fan wall, and a strict no-lying policy.
power: Mains power, plus the waste heat of the cards under test, which is the entire point.
failure: Quiet fan curve plus a sick card equals a thermal shutdown and one card promoted to paperweight.
transcript: The chamber does not grade on a curve. Either the card holds boost or it does not. Everything else is commentary.

purposes: Catches virtual registers the moment the allocator spills them, before they hit the cold stack.
Keeps spilled values warm in a LIFO cozy so reloads come back at register-adjacent temperatures.
Auditions spilled registers for re-promotion when a physical register frees up mid-function.
built: A coffee can, a butterfly net, a LIFO buffer wired from doorbell parts, and a label maker.
power: Scavenged from the spill itself: every store to the stack trickle-charges a capacitor.
failure: A net with a hole drops spilled values into the void. They return as NaN and nobody apologizes.
transcript: Caught seventeen spills during a crypto round last Tuesday. Zero reached the stack. One register asked to stay in the can permanently. Request denied, it had work to do.

purposes: Erects interference fences between virtual registers whose live ranges overlap.
Patrols the fence line and sounds a klaxon when two neighbors reach for the same physical register.
Negotiates treaties: one register spills voluntarily in exchange for priority reloading.
built: Survey stakes, a spool of actual barbed wire, a klaxon from a decommissioned forklift, and diplomacy.
power: A hand crank. The fence is a moral construct, it does not need electricity, only commitment.
failure: During the graveyard shift the klaxon stuck on and negotiated with itself until sunrise.
transcript: Fence held through a fifteen-register crypto round with two orderly spills. The klaxon has been retired with honors and now guards the paint booth.
